chapters.title: Chapter 4: Alternative and Real Assets Through the Cycle

lessons.title: Cash and Money Market Instruments: The Underrated Cycle Asset

body.text: Cash is the one asset class every chapter so far has treated as a leftover. It deserves better: it is the only asset that earns a positive, rising, zero-volatility return in the cycle's toughest quadrant, and it is the option that lets you buy every other asset class cheap when its turn comes.

children.text: Back in Chapter 1's growth-inflation grid, stagflation, falling growth with rising inflation, was flagged as the quadrant where cash usually leads. This lesson explains why, and gives cash a fair, two-sided treatment: it has a real benefit most investors underrate, and a real cost most investors also underrate.
Cash Is a Call Option on Every Other Asset Class

Every crash you've studied in this course created a buying opportunity for whoever had cash ready to deploy. The FY21 recovery that followed the Covid crash, the equity rebound after the taper tantrum, gold's rally once real rates collapsed in mid-2020, all of these rewarded investors who had kept some dry powder through the panic and punished investors who were fully invested with nothing left to buy the dip. Cash's biggest value is often not its own return, it is the option it gives you to buy other assets when they're cheap.

body.title: Two Investors, March 2020
body.scenario: In February 2020, two investors each hold a ₹10 lakh portfolio. Investor A is 100% invested in equities. Investor B holds 80% equities and keeps 20% (₹2 lakh) in a liquid fund. The Covid crash hits in March 2020, and both portfolios fall sharply. Investor B deploys the full ₹2 lakh into equities near the bottom of the crash.
body.prompt: Using what you know about the FY21 recovery from Chapter 1, roughly how would you expect the two portfolios to compare a year later, and what is the actual source of Investor B's advantage?
body.modelAnswer: Both portfolios would have recovered strongly given the roughly 70% Nifty rally in FY21, but Investor B's advantage comes specifically from the ₹2 lakh redeployed near the bottom, which would have captured a much larger share of that rebound than money that stayed invested throughout the fall and rise. The source of the advantage isn't that cash itself outperformed, the liquid fund barely moved, it's that holding cash created the option to buy the dip, an option Investor A didn't have. The same 20% cash allocation would have looked like a drag on returns in any year the market simply went straight up, which is the real cost of holding this option.

children.text: The Other Side: Cash's Real Cost Is Inflation

Fixed deposit interest is taxed as regular income at your slab rate, unlike the more favourable long-term capital gains treatment on equity. Over the last decade, average one-year FD rates at major Indian banks have generally run somewhere in the 5.5% to 7% range, while CPI inflation has averaged roughly 5% to 6% over the same stretch. For an investor in a higher tax bracket, the after-tax FD return has often barely kept pace with inflation, and in some years has lagged it outright. Cash preserves nominal rupees with near-total certainty. It does not reliably preserve purchasing power.

children.text: Why Cash Wins the Stagflation Quadrant, and Where Gold Still Beats It

In stagflation, equities struggle as margins compress (Chapter 2), and bonds struggle as inflation and possible rate hikes hurt duration, with credit spreads sometimes widening on top (Chapter 3). Cash and short-term money market instruments have a specific edge here: as the RBI raises rates to fight inflation, a liquid fund's yield resets upward within weeks, delivering a rising, positive nominal return with essentially no price volatility. Gold, covered in the last lesson, is actually the stronger inflation hedge in this quadrant on a real, after-inflation basis, but it comes with genuine price volatility, including the kind of sharp drawdown you saw in gold's initial reaction to the March 2020 panic. Cash's edge over gold isn't a bigger return, it's certainty: no drawdown risk at all while you wait out the storm.
Completing the 2022 Picture: What Cash Actually Earned

Chapter 1's exercise on 2022 covered equities (up only modestly, a real loss after inflation), long-duration bond funds (down, as yields rose), and gold (up by low double digits in INR terms). Cash completes the picture. As the RBI raised the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50% across 2022 into early 2023, liquid fund and fresh FD yields rose right along with it, delivering a rising, positive nominal return with none of the NAV volatility that hit long-duration bond funds.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Rates are widely expected to keep rising over the next year. Which of the following best captures that rising-rate environment with the least amount of price volatility?
options: It doesn't matter, all instruments respond the same way
body.explanation: A liquid fund's near-zero duration means its NAV barely moves with rate changes, and its yield resets upward quickly as rates rise. A long-duration gilt fund would take a real price hit in the same environment, exactly the duration risk covered in Chapter 3.

body.text: Cash and FDs are the right tool for a rising-rate environment, not a falling one. When a rate-cutting cycle begins, an FD that matures and rolls over locks in a progressively lower rate each time, a real reinvestment risk, while a long-duration bond fund actually gains from falling yields, exactly the phase-based duration call from Chapter 3. Holding too much cash through an entire cutting cycle means missing the capital gains that longer-duration bonds are built to capture in that phase.

cards.definition: A short-term debt instrument, typically maturing within a year, such as T-Bills, commercial paper, and certificates of deposit.
A short-term (91, 182, or 364-day) government security, sovereign-backed and carrying minimal duration given its short tenure.
The risk that a maturing fixed deposit or bond has to be reinvested at a lower prevailing interest rate, typically a concern during a rate-cutting cycle.
Cash or liquid holdings kept available specifically to be deployed into other assets when opportunities, such as a market crash, arise.

points: Cash's biggest value is often the option it creates to buy other assets cheap during a panic, not its own standalone return, as the FY21 recovery and gold's mid-2020 rally both showed
Cash and FDs carry a real, underrated cost: FD interest is taxed at your income slab rate, and after-tax returns have often barely kept pace with, or lagged, CPI inflation over the last decade
Liquid and overnight funds carry near-zero duration and reset their yield quickly as rates change, while FDs carry reinvestment risk when they mature and roll over
Cash wins the stagflation quadrant on certainty, a rising, positive nominal return with zero drawdown, even though gold is typically the stronger real, inflation-adjusted hedge in the same quadrant

In the 2022 hiking cycle, liquid fund and FD yields rose from around 3.5-4% to around 6.5-7%, completing a four-asset picture for that year alongside modestly positive equities, negative long-duration bonds, and gains in gold
Cash is the right tool heading into a rising-rate phase and the wrong one to over-hold through a falling-rate phase, when longer-duration bonds are built to capture the bigger gain
